planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or again in late summer for a fall crop; Kyona regrows quickly after cut-and-come-again harvest.

directions: Sow seed thinly a quarter inch deep in rich, well-drained soil and thin seedlings to reduce crowding once established. This selected mizuna strain produces dense clumps of finely serrated, feathery dark-green leaves with slender white stalks and holds flavor well without becoming overly pungent. Harvest outer leaves continually for salads and stir-fries, or cut the whole plant an inch above the crown for regrowth. Bolts in sustained heat, so it performs best as a spring or autumn crop.

planting.note: Give plants more room than standard mizuna since Waido forms noticeably larger, more upright rosettes; also suited to a late-summer sowing for fall harvest.

directions: Waido, meaning wide leaf in Japanese, is a larger-statured mizuna selection bred for bunching markets, with broader, less deeply cut leaves than standard mizuna and thicker, crisp petioles. Direct sow into fertile soil and keep evenly moist to encourage tender, mild-flavored growth. Whole heads can be cut for bunching or leaves picked individually for stir-fries and hot pot greens. Cold-hardy and slow to bolt compared to smaller mizuna types, making it a good choice for extended fall harvest.

common_name: Scarlet Frills Mustard (Deep Maroon Frilled Mustard)

planting.note: Sow in early spring or late summer; cooler temperatures deepen the maroon color and mellow the mustard's heat.

directions: This ornamental-edible mustard produces deeply fringed, almost lacy leaves in a rich burgundy-maroon that intensifies in cool weather and full sun. Direct sow into loose, fertile soil and thin to final spacing, using thinnings as spicy microgreens. Leaves can be harvested young for salad mix, where the color and frilled texture stand out, or left to mature for a peppery cooked green. Plants are attractive enough for mixed ornamental beds as well as the vegetable garden, but bolt quickly once summer heat arrives.

planting.note: Best harvested young as a baby-leaf salad green; the horseradish-like bite intensifies as leaves mature and in warmer weather.

directions: Wasabina is a mizuna-type mustard green selected for a sharp, wasabi-like bite that adds punch to salad mixes without needing actual wasabi root. Direct sow shallowly into rich soil and grow as a cut-and-come-again crop, snipping the glossy, deeply serrated leaves at baby size for the mildest, most versatile flavor. It thrives in cool spring and fall conditions and tends to bolt in summer heat, so succession sow every few weeks for continuous harvest. Use sparingly as a spicy accent in mesclun mixes, sandwiches, or sushi-style garnishes.

common_name: Miike Giant Mustard (Giant Red Japanese Heirloom Mustard)

planting.note: Give plants ample room to reach full size; also excellent sown in late summer for a fall crop, as cool weather deepens the bronze-red color.

directions: Miike Giant is a Japanese heirloom mustard prized for its huge, savoyed leaves that emerge green and develop striking bronze-purple coloring and deep-cut, ruffled margins as they mature. Direct sow into fertile soil and thin generously, since mature plants form large, dramatic rosettes over two feet across. Young leaves are milder and good raw, while mature leaves carry substantial heat and are best braised, stir-fried, or used in kimchi-style ferments. The plant's size and color also make it a striking addition to ornamental vegetable plantings.

common_name: Green in the Snow Mustard (Xue Li Hong)

planting.note: Exceptionally cold-hardy; sow in late summer for a fall and winter harvest that survives frost and light snow, or in early spring for a quicker crop.

directions: This traditional Chinese mustard, known as xue li hong, meaning red amid the snow, is grown specifically for its ability to keep producing tender, deeply toothed serrated leaves through hard frosts and light snow cover. Direct sow into fertile soil in late summer for the best cold-season crop, harvesting leaves continually as a cut-and-come-again green. Leaves develop a purplish tinge and a distinctive sharp, mustardy tang in cold weather, and are traditionally salted or lightly fermented as a pickle as well as used fresh in soups and stir-fries. Its extreme hardiness makes it one of the last leafy greens standing in an unheated winter garden.

common_name: Tokyo Cross Turnip (AAS-Winning Hybrid Salad Turnip)

planting.note: Sow directly as soon as soil can be worked, and again in late summer for fall roots; thin early since this hybrid grows fast and can crowd itself.

directions: Tokyo Cross is a fast-maturing F1 hybrid turnip, an All-America Selections winner bred from the open-pollinated Tokyo Market type, valued for producing smooth, pure-white globes that stay tender, mild, and crack-free even if left in the ground past ideal size. Direct sow shallowly into loose soil and thin to a few inches apart, keeping the bed consistently moist for the fastest, sweetest roots. Both the crisp roots and the tender young tops are edible, making it a dual-purpose crop for salads, quick pickles, or braising greens. Its speed and heat tolerance for a turnip make it well suited to succession planting through much of the season.
